transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-25
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Moreno (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Jordan Li (Redwood CSM); Samira Khan (Greybridge Platform), Tom Delgado (SRE), Evan Liu (Head of ML), Rita Morales (Security)

Summary: Quick sync on the pilot stability after last week's 5xx spike, walked through timeout / rate-windowing suggestions, agreed on benchmark and VPC/KMS deep-dive.

Topics: 5xx surge analysis, client retry budgets, rate windowing, KV cache warmup, VPC cross-account KMS, next steps and owners.

[00:00] Alex: Hey everybody, thanks for joining. we have about 50 minutes, want to do a quick recap of last week's incident, share a couple tuning knobs and then agree on a short benchmark and next steps. Samira you want to kick off with what you saw?
[00:18] Samira: yeah uh thanks Alex. so on Tuesday at around 09:42 our latency crawled and we started to see intermittent 502/503s and some 504 timeouts. The pattern seemed correlated with a few heavy user jobs and then a second wave when backups kicked in, so maybe a hotkey type surge?
[00:34] Tom: right, and to add, our sidecar showed a burst of long tail request RTTs to the Redwood endpoint, then our client retried aggressively which amplified the window. we had a brief period of connection queue depth rising.
[00:48] Priya: OK, brief clarifying q — when you say 'aggressively' do you have retry counts and backoff details? is it immediate three retries? linear backoff?
[00:57] Tom: it was basically immediate 3 retries with 200ms base, no jitter. so basically synchronized retry waves.
[01:08] Evan: also worth noting our workload has some long context requests for multi-document summarization, so tokenization / kv-cache warmup hits matter — cold KV cache meant longer first token latencies.
[01:20] Alex: got it. so two amplifiers: client retry pattern and cold KV cache on the model side. we want to address both with client-side retry guidance and server-side rate windowing / circuit-breaker.
[01:32] Samira: yes. can you walk us through what Redwood recommends for the retry budget versus backoff? and also the rate windows idea you mentioned in the slack note.
[01:42] Priya: sure. recommended pattern: small retry budget per request path — e.g. 2 retries max for idempotent calls, exponential backoff with jitter (start 250ms, x2, cap 2s). more importantly use a token bucket style client-side limiter so you don't regenerate huge fan-out. on the server we apply rate-windowing: short window (1-3s) with adaptive admission that measures queue depth and kv-cache hit rate. when queue depth crosses threshold we start shedding non-critical requests (low-priority routes) and favor cached prefixes.
[02:20] Rita: about shedding — does that mean Redwood will return 429 for low-priority routes? we need to make sure SREs and product teams can map those responses appropriately. also need to confirm that audit logs show the reason codes for sheds for compliance.
[02:35] Priya: yep we tag responses with a reason and include it in telemetry (e.g., X-Redwood-Overload: rate_window_shed). audit logs include decisions, and Jordan can share the log retention doc.
[02:47] Jordan: quick note — retention is currently 90 days for trial telemetry; enterprise can extend. I'll attach the security packet with the specific fields that appear in logs.
[02:58] Samira: ok thanks. can you also confirm how KV cache is populated? our heavy flows open long contexts, there's a lot of unique prefixes which makes warmup harder.
[03:10] Priya: right, KV cache is populated per active sequence and is sticky for the model instance. we recommend warmup probes — lightweight prefix-only calls to prime cache before big jobs. we can also enable prefetching on the runtime for known job patterns. but there is a cost tradeoff.
[03:28] Tom: is there an out-of-the-box warmup script? we could run one as a pre-job step if you provide sample payloads.
[03:36] Alex: we have a small open-source probe script and a runbook. Alex: i'll share that link after the call — it's the one we use in Dedicated pilots.
[03:44] Samira: great. on the spike telemetry you mentioned a 503 pattern tied to host eviction during autoscale — we saw nodes doing some brief restarts, was that thermal or scheduler?
[03:54] Priya: on Redwood's side logs show it was preemptible-like spot eviction on our internal test cluster we used for this pilot window; but for your Dedicated pilot we can pin instance types and set graceful drain windows so you don't hit the eviction pattern.
[04:12] Evan: question on SSO and VPC — Rita and I talked about key management. if we run Private deployment with our KMS, what does the handshake look like? any CRL or cross-account role we need?
[04:23] Priya: for VPC + Customer-managed KMS we do an IAM role assumption pattern and use envelope encryption; keys never leave your account. there are a few steps: establish cross-account role, exchange metadata, and configure either AWS KMS or HSM. we'll walk through with your security team.
[04:40] Rita: we need SOC2 controls on the envelope key usage logs and proof of no-key egress. can Redwood produce those artifacts?
[04:48] Jordan: yes; we have an SOC2 package and HSM attestations for enterprise. I'll attach the certs and the KMS integration checklist.
[04:58] Samira: good. back to rate-windowing — can Priya show the tuning knobs you suggested and the expected effect on latency tail?
[05:08] Priya: sure. quick demo — (note: small pause) imagine a sliding window of 2s. we track requests entering the serving queue, and we compute a moving average tail latency. If average tail goes above SLO, we start rate-windowing by lowering admission via multiplicative factor, and we favor cached requests. That converts large spikes into graceful degradation — some requests are 429 fast, rather than many 502/504. Expected outcome: lower 5xx count, slightly higher early-429s.
[05:40] Tom: that's acceptable as long as client can respect 429 and back off. the problem last week was 429 wasn't honored because our client lib treated it as retryable. that config is on us so we will change that.
[05:52] Alex: perfect. small checklist — update client lib to treat 429 as non-retryable for non-idempotent workloads or apply Retry-After logic. Priya will provide recommended headers.
[06:05] Samira: about metrics — what telemetry do we need to monitor to know windowing is engaged?
[06:12] Priya: watch queue depth, kv-cache hit rate, early_429 rate, 5xx rate, and token generation latency (p50/p95/p99). We'll provide a dashboard template.
[06:24] Evan: can we also get per-route token cost breakdown? we need to show exec teams the cost delta if we run warmup and prefetch.
[06:31] Alex: yes, we'll break down cost per-token with and without prefetch and share a small model.
[06:37] Samira: earlier you mentioned 'firebreak' — what exactly does that do? is that the same as circuit-breaker?
[06:43] Priya: shorthand — firebreak is an aggressive circuit-breaker state we enter under sustained overload to protect core latency SLOs. it forces low-priority routes to error-fast with explicit metadata so clients can fall back to a degraded path.
[06:58] Tom: ok, practical ask — can Redwood provide a run where we replay our 10-minute peak with our real payloads so we can see behavior under the burst?
[07:06] Priya: yes, we can run a replay in our staging and produce a replay report with per-host metrics. ideally you share the payloads and a traffic window.
[07:14] Samira: we'll do that. we'll sanitize payloads and upload via S3 link.
[07:19] Jordan: i'll send the upload instructions after the call.
[07:23] Alex: great. quick pause — any other blockers from security? Rita?
[07:27] Rita: main blocker is KMS attestation and proof that telemetry doesn't leak PII. we need a short architecture diagram with data flows and where keys live.
[07:36] Alex: Jordan and I will produce a short diagram for you.
[07:39] Rita: also we need retention settings and how to request redaction.
[07:43] Jordan: noted.
[07:45] (brief cross talk)
[07:50] Priya: ok going back to tuning — here's recommended initial config for the POC: client-side retry cap 2, jittered exponential backoff start 250ms cap 2s; server-side window length 2s, queue depth threshold 120, kv-cache prefetch enabled for heavy jobs, and a gradual 20% admission cut when threshold exceeded. we should run the replay and then iterate.
[08:12] Samira: question about the queue depth unit — is that per-host or cluster-wide?
[08:18] Priya: per-host admission controller, but we report cluster-wide aggregates too.
[08:23] Tom: on the cluster we saw a single host hit 300 queue depth due to uneven routing, could be hotkey. is there a recommended routing fix?
[08:33] Priya: yes we can enable request hashing on prefixes to spread hot keys and enable sticky split across instances. but if a single job uses unique prefixes it's tricky — warmup helps there.
[08:42] Evan: about warmup cost — if we run probes at scale will that blow our token bill? how do we estimate?
[08:48] Alex: we will provide a cost estimate: probes are short and you can choose frequency; example: priming 50k prefixes once per hour with a tiny token count is X dollars — we'll calculate with your payloads.
[08:58] Samira: good. one more item — last incident had a 15-minute recovery window where tail stayed high even after traffic dropped. is that related to KV cache TTL?
[09:08] Priya: possibly. we saw in logs the cache churn and cold starts on new hosts, which can cause elevated p99 for a bit. increasing cache TTL per model instance or pre-warming new instances helps. we'll show you tuning knobs.
[09:22] Tom: on the subject of backoff in client, we will change our SDK to introduce jitter and also include a token bucket limiter for burst protection. we'll share the PR.
[09:31] Alex: excellent. Next — benchmarks: we propose two runs: 1) replay of your exact 10-minute peak; 2) synthetic 15-minute burst with 3x concurrency to validate firebreak behavior. We'll run both and share the replay report and CSVs.
[09:47] Samira: timeline realistic? when can you run?
[09:50] Priya: we can run the first replay within 24-48 hours after you upload payloads. synthetic within 72 hours.
[09:58] Samira: agreed. we'll aim to upload today.
[10:01] (pause)
[10:05] Alex: let's talk briefly about fallback strategies — for low-priority requests we recommend two-tier fallback: first try a smaller quantized model variant (faster, cheaper), second return cached response or a safe degraded summary.
[10:19] Evan: quantized models sometimes change output distribution — we need to run A/B on quality. can Redwood run side-by-side evals?
[10:27] Priya: yes, we have autosampling eval harness to compare model outputs. we can attach a quality threshold and only promote fallback if it meets tolerance.
[10:36] Samira: please do that. we'll provide prompt sets.
[10:39] Tom: small security follow-up — regarding 429 codes, our infra currently treats 429 as retryable. we will change it. can you embed Retry-After and a hazard header so we can programmatically distinguish?
[10:50] Priya: yes we support Retry-After and X-Redwood-Reason and a numeric code in an extra header.
[10:56] Jordan: i'll include the header spec in follow-up.
[11:00] Samira: anything else on the runbook?
[11:03] Alex: two final asks: 1) we'll provide the warmup script and cost calc; 2) Priya will provide the default rate-window config and the dashboard template.
[11:12] Samira: sounds good.
[11:14] Evan: on reporting — after you run replays can you include p50/p95/p99 and also per-route 429/5xx counts? we want CSVs to ingest into our monitoring.
[11:25] Priya: yes we'll deliver CSVs and the dashboard link.
[11:29] Rita: and please include the KMS architecture doc and SOC2 artifacts in the follow-up.
[11:34] Jordan: we'll bundle security artifacts and runbook in one package.
[11:38] Alex: ok let's recap next steps — Alex to run benchmark and share, Priya to share tuning notes and dashboard, Jordan to send upload and security docs, Greybridge to upload payloads and change SDK retry behavior. agreed?
[11:52] Samira: agreed.
[11:55] Tom: agreed.
[11:57] Alex: thanks everyone. we'll reconvene after the replay results — suggest Thursday sync if that works.
[12:04] Evan: Thursday works.
[12:06] Rita: thanks all.
